title: Getting Started with Audio Programming (Through Building a Terminal Guitar Amp)
description: A beginner-friendly introduction to audio programming concepts through building a simple terminal-based guitar amp using ALSA.

content.text: Audio programming is really complicated, and I definitely don’t know enough to explain everything. But I can explain what helped me get started. That’s what this post is — just the things that finally made stuff click for me.
Why I Started This

I wanted to do something fun with both guitar and programming, so I decided to build a simple guitar amp in the terminal. I had worked with audio before, but only through really abstracted libraries where you don’t see what’s actually going on.

This was my first time actually dealing with audio at a lower level. I ended up using libasound2 (ALSA), which was probably more complicated than I needed, but it forced me to actually understand what was happening.
What an Audio Interface Actually Does

An audio interface is just a device that lets your computer send and receive audio. The important part is that audio in the real world is analog (a continuously changing voltage), but computers only understand digital data (bits).
So something has to convert between those two worlds. That’s basically the entire job of the interface.
Buffers (This Is Where Things Start Making Sense)

When audio comes in from something like a guitar, the interface converts it into digital data and stores it in a hardware buffer. Once enough data is collected, it interrupts the computer and says “hey, come grab this.”
For output, it’s the opposite. The interface says “hey, I have space,” and the computer fills the buffer with audio data.
One important thing: these buffers are circular. So when they reach the end, they wrap back around to the beginning. It’s basically like indexing an array with modulo.
Also, input and output are completely separate — you have a capture buffer and a playback buffer running at the same time.
PCM (You’ll See This Everywhere)
PCM stands for Pulse Code Modulation. It’s just raw, uncompressed digital audio. In ALSA, "PCM" basically just means "audio stream" most of the time.
XRUNs (aka When Everything Breaks)
An XRUN is when your program can’t keep up with the audio stream in real time.

Underrun: playback needs data, but there isn’t any ready.
Overrun: input has data, but there’s nowhere to put it.
Both of these usually mean glitches, popping, or just broken audio.
Where ALSA Fits
The way I think about ALSA is kind of like how OpenGL fits in graphics.
Program → libasound2 → ALSA → audio hardware
That’s not exactly how it works anymore, but it’s a useful mental model starting out.
Modern Linux Audio (PipeWire)
In reality, most modern Linux systems use PipeWire now. It sits in the middle and manages all audio (and video) streams.
So what’s actually happening is more like:
Program → libasound2 → PipeWire → kernel driver → hardware
The reason your ALSA code still works is because PipeWire is designed to support it.

Conclusion

This stuff felt super confusing at first, especially all the buffer and system-level details. But once I understood how data actually moves — from the guitar, into a buffer, into my program — it started to feel way more manageable.
I’m still figuring a lot of this out, but building something small like a terminal guitar amp made it way easier to learn than just reading docs.
